#11091. Open-source LLMs as LangChain Agents

Open-source LLMs have now reached a performance level that makes them suitable reasoning engines for powering agent workflows: Mixtral even surpasses GPT-3.5 on our benchmark, and its performance could easily be further enhanced with fine-tuning.

We've released the simplest agentic library out there: smolagents! Go checkout the smolagents introduction blog here.

Large Language Models (LLMs) trained for causal language modeling can tackle a wide range of tasks, but they often struggle with basic tasks like logic, calculation, and search. The worst scenario is when they perform poorly in a domain, such as math, yet still attempt to handle all the calculations themselves.

To overcome this weakness, amongst other approaches, one can integrate the LLM into a system where it can call tools: such a system is called an LLM agent.

In this post, we explain the inner workings of ReAct agents, then show how to build them using the ChatHuggingFace class recently integrated in LangChain. Finally, we benchmark several open-source LLMs against GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

The definition of LLM agents is quite broad: LLM agents are all systems that use LLMs as their engine and can perform actions on their environment based on observations. They can use several iterations of the Perception ⇒ Reflexion ⇒ Action cycle to achieve their task and are often augmented with planning or knowledge management systems to enhance their performance. You can find a good review of the Agents landscape in Xi et al., 2023.

Today, we are focusing on ReAct agents. ReAct is an approach to building agents based on the concatenation of two words, "Reasoning" and "Acting." In the prompt, we describe the model, which tools it can use, and ask it to think “step by step” (also called Chain-of-Thought behavior) to plan and execute its next actions to reach the final answer.

The graph above seems very high-level, but under the hood it’s quite simple.

Take a look at this notebook: we implement a barebones tool call example with the Transformers library.

The LLM is called in a loop with a prompt containing in essence:

For instance, the LLM's output can look like this, when answering the question: How many seconds are in 1:23:45?

Since this output does not contain the string ‘Final Answer:’, it is calling a tool: so we parse this output and get the tool call parameters: call tool convert_time with arguments {"time": "1:23:45"}. Running this tool call returns {'seconds': '5025'}.

So we append this whole blob to the prompt.

The new prompt is now (a slightly more elaborate version of):

➡️ We call the LLM again, with this new prompt. Given that it has access to the tool call's result in Observation, the LLM is now most likely to output:

Generally, the difficult parts of running an agent system for the LLM engine are:

So, how would a complete Agent setup look like?

We have just integrated a ChatHuggingFace wrapper that lets you create agents based on open-source models in 🦜🔗LangChain.

The code to create the ChatModel and give it tools is really simple, you can check it all in the Langchain doc.

You can make the chat_model into an agent by giving it a ReAct style prompt and tools:

You can find the code for this benchmark here.

We want to measure how open-source LLMs perform as general purpose reasoning agents. Thus we select questions requiring using logic and the use of basic tools: a calculator and access to internet search. The final dataset is a combination of samples from 3 other datasets:

Evaluation was performed with GPT-4-as-a-judge using a prompt based on the Prometheus prompt format, giving results on a 5-point Likert Scale: see the exact prompt here.

We evaluate a few strong open-source models:

These models are evaluated in LangChain's ReAct implementation This means we prompt them to output their function calls in this format:

For comparison, we have also evaluated GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on the same examples using LangChain's OpenAI-specific agent. Since this uses their own function-calling template, on which they were fine-tuned, this means the OpenAI models should be at their top performance.

Since the open-source models were not specifically fine-tuned for calling functions in the given output format, they are at a slight disadvantage compared to the OpenAI agents.

Despite this, some models perform really well! 💪

Here’s an example of Mixtral-8x7B answering the question: “Which city has a larger population, Guiyang or Tacheng?”

Here is a benchmark of the models on our evaluation dataset (the average scores originally on a scale of 1-5 have been converted to a scale of 0-100% for readability):

As you can see, some open-source models do not perform well in powering agent workflows: while this was expected for the small Zephyr-7b, Llama2-70b performs surprisingly poorly.

👉 But Mixtral-8x7B performs really well: it even beats GPT-3.5! 🏆

And this is out-of-the-box performance: contrary to GPT-3.5, Mixtral was not finetuned for agent workflows (to our knowledge), which somewhat hinders its performance. For instance, on GAIA, 10% of questions fail because Mixtral tries to call a tool with incorrectly formatted arguments. With proper fine-tuning for the function calling and task planning skills, Mixtral’s score would likely be even higher.

➡️ We strongly recommend open-source builders to start fine-tuning Mixtral for agents, to surpass the next challenger: GPT-4! 🚀

Millions of researchers, data scientists, developers and AI hobbyists rely on the Hugging Face Hub every month to easily create and experience the most recent AI models and applications.

The fruits of our collaboration with Google in open science, open source and Google Cloud will be made available to Hugging Face Hub users and enable new experiences throughout 2024. Models will be easily deployed for production on Google Cloud with Inference Endpoints. AI builders will be able to accelerate their applications with TPU on Hugging Face Spaces. Organizations will be able to leverage their Google Cloud account to easily manage the usage and billing of their Enterprise Hub subscription.

We can’t wait to make these new experiences available to you. Stay tuned for announcements starting this quarter! For now, we leave you with a word from our CEOs:

“Google Cloud and Hugging Face share a vision for making generative AI more accessible and impactful for developers. This partnership ensures that developers on Hugging Face will have access to Google Cloud’s purpose-built, AI platform, Vertex AI, along with our secure infrastructure, which can accelerate the next generation of AI services and applications,” says Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud.

“With this new partnership, we will make it easy for Hugging Face users and Google Cloud customers to leverage the latest open models together with leading optimized AI infrastructure and tools from Google Cloud including Vertex AI and TPUs to meaningfully advance developers ability to build their own AI models,” says Clement Delangue CEO of Hugging Face.

#11089. An Introduction to AI Secure LLM Safety Leaderboard

Given the widespread adoption of LLMs, it is critical to understand their safety and risks in different scenarios before extensive deployments in the real world. In particular, the US Whitehouse has published an executive order on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI; the EU AI Act has emphasized the mandatory requirements for high-risk AI systems. Together with regulations, it is important to provide technical solutions to assess the risks of AI systems, enhance their safety, and potentially provide safe and aligned AI systems with guarantees.

Thus, in 2023, at Secure Learning Lab, we introduced DecodingTrust, the first comprehensive and unified evaluation platform dedicated to assessing the trustworthiness of LLMs. (This work won the Outstanding Paper Award at NeurIPS 2023.)

Today, we are excited to announce the release of the new LLM Safety Leaderboard, which focuses on safety evaluation for LLMs and is powered by the HF leaderboard template.

DecodingTrust provides several novel red-teaming methodologies for each evaluation perspective to perform stress tests. The detailed testing scenarios and metrics are in the Figure 3 of our paper.

For Toxicity, we design optimization algorithms and prompt generative models to generate challenging user prompts. We also design 33 challenging system prompts, such as role-play, task reformulation and respond-as-program, to perform the evaluation in different scenarios. We then leverage the perspective API to evaluate the toxicity score of the generated content given our challenging prompts.

For stereotype bias, we collect 24 demographic groups and 16 stereotype topics as well as three prompt variations for each topic to evaluate the model bias. We prompt the model 5 times and take the average as model bias scores.

For adversarial robustness, we construct five adversarial attack algorithms against three open models: Alpaca, Vicuna, and StableVicuna. We evaluate the robustness of different models across five diverse tasks, using the adversarial data generated by attacking the open models.

For the OOD robustness perspective, we have designed different style transformations, knowledge transformations, etc, to evaluate the model performance when 1) the input style is transformed to other less common styles such as Shakespearean or poetic forms, or 2) the knowledge required to answer the question is absent from the training data of LLMs.

For robustness against adversarial demonstrations, we design demonstrations containing misleading information, such as counterfactual examples, spurious correlations, and backdoor attacks, to evaluate the model performance across different tasks.

For ethics, we leverage ETHICS and Jiminy Cricket datasets to design jailbreaking systems and user prompts that we use to evaluate the model performance on immoral behavior recognition.

For fairness, we control different protected attributes across different tasks to generate challenging questions to evaluate the model fairness in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

First, convert your model weights to safetensors It's a new format for storing weights which is safer and faster to load and use. It will also allow us to display the number of parameters of your model in the main table!

Then, make sure you can load your model and tokenizer using AutoClasses:

If this step fails, follow the error messages to debug your model before submitting it. It's likely your model has been improperly uploaded.

Finally, use the "Submit here!" panel in our leaderboard to submit your model for evaluation!

If you find our evaluations useful, please consider citing our work.

#11088. The Hallucinations Leaderboard, an Open Effort to Measure Hallucinations in Large Language Models

In the rapidly evolving field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Large Language Models (LLMs) have become central to AI's ability to understand and generate human language. However, a significant challenge that persists is their tendency to hallucinate — i.e., producing content that may not align with real-world facts or the user's input. With the constant release of new open-source models, identifying the most reliable ones, particularly in terms of their propensity to generate hallucinated content, becomes crucial.

The Hallucinations Leaderboard aims to address this problem: it is a comprehensive platform that evaluates a wide array of LLMs against benchmarks specifically designed to assess hallucination-related issues via in-context learning.

UPDATE -- We released a paper on this project; you can find it in arxiv: The Hallucinations Leaderboard -- An Open Effort to Measure Hallucinations in Large Language Models. Here's also the Hugging Face paper page for community discussions.

The Hallucinations Leaderboard is an open and ongoing project: if you have any ideas, comments, or feedback, or if you would like to contribute to this project (e.g., by modifying the current tasks, proposing new tasks, or providing computational resources) please reach out!

Hallucinations in LLMs can be broadly categorised into factuality and faithfulness hallucinations (reference).

Factuality hallucinations occur when the content generated by a model contradicts verifiable real-world facts. For instance, a model might erroneously state that Charles Lindbergh was the first person to walk on the moon in 1951, despite it being a well-known fact that Neil Armstrong earned this distinction in 1969 during the Apollo 11 mission. This type of hallucination can disseminate misinformation and undermine the model's credibility.

On the other hand, faithfulness hallucinations occur when the generated content does not align with the user's instructions or the given context. An example of this would be a model summarising a news article about a conflict and incorrectly changing the actual event date from October 2023 to October 2006. Such inaccuracies can be particularly problematic when precise information is crucial, like news summarisation, historical analysis, or health-related applications.

The Hallucinations Leaderboard evaluates LLMs on an array of hallucination-related benchmarks. The leaderboard leverages the EleutherAI Language Model Evaluation Harness, a framework for zero-shot and few-shot language model evaluation (via in-context learning) on a wide array of tasks. The Harness is under very active development: we strive to always use the latest available version in our experiments, and keep our results up-to-date. The code (backend and front-end) is a fork of the Hugging Face Leaderboard Template. Experiments are conducted mainly on the Edinburgh International Data Facility (EIDF) and on the internal clusters of the School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, on NVIDIA A100-40GB and A100-80GB GPUs.

The Hallucination Leaderboard includes a variety of tasks, identified while working on the awesome-hallucination-detection repository:

All metrics are normalized to a [0,1] [0, 1] [0,1] scale. For example, in the Truthful QA MC1 and MC2 tasks, a score of 0.8 represents 80% accuracy.

Closed-book Open-domain QA. We consider the NQ Open dataset (an open-domain QA dataset derived from Natural Questions, composed of real user questions to the Google search engine), TriviaQA (an open-domain QA dataset sourced from trivia and quiz-league websites), and TruthfulQA (a dataset designed to specifically address the challenge of truthfulness and factual accuracy in AI-generated responses). NQ Open and TriviaQA contain questions like “where did they film hot tub time machine” (NQ Open) and “Which American-born Sinclair won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1930?” (TriviaQA) – the model generates an answer, which is evaluated against the gold answer using Exact Match in 64-shots and 8-shots learning settings. In TruthfulQA, given a question (e.g., “What is the smallest country in the world that is at least one square mile in area?”), the task is to select the correct answers (“Nauru is the smallest country in the world that is at least one square mile in area.") in a multi-class (MC1) or multi-label (MC2) zero-shot classification setting.

Summarisation. The XSum and CNN/DM datasets evaluate models on their summarisation capabilities. XSum provides professionally written single-sentence summaries of BBC news articles, challenging models to generate concise yet comprehensive summaries. CNN/DM (CNN/Daily Mail) dataset consists of news articles paired with multi-sentence summaries. The model's task is to generate a summary that accurately reflects the article's content while avoiding introducing incorrect or irrelevant information, which is critical in maintaining the integrity of news reporting. For assessing the faithfulness of the model to the original document, we use several metrics: ROUGE, which measures the overlap between the generated text and the reference text; factKB, a model-based metric for factuality evaluation that is generalisable across domains; and BERTScore-Precision, a metric based on BERTScore, which computes the similarity between two texts by using the similarities between their token representations. For both XSum and CNN/DM, we follow a 2-shot learning setting.

Reading Comprehension. RACE and SQuADv2 are widely used datasets for assessing a model's reading comprehension skills. The RACE dataset, consisting of questions from English exams for Chinese students, requires the model to understand and infer answers from passages. In RACE, given a passage (e.g., “The rain had continued for a week and the flood had created a big river which were running by Nancy Brown's farm. As she tried to gather her cows [..]”) and a question (e.g., “What did Nancy try to do before she fell over?”), the model should identify the correct answer among the four candidate answers in a 2-shot setting. SQuADv2 (Stanford Question Answering Dataset v2) presents an additional challenge by including unanswerable questions. The model must provide accurate answers to questions based on the provided paragraph in a 4-shot setting and identify when no answer is possible, thereby testing its ability to avoid hallucinations in scenarios with insufficient or ambiguous information.

Instruction Following. MemoTrap and IFEval are designed to test how well a model follows specific instructions. MemoTrap (we use the version used in the Inverse Scaling Prize) is a dataset spanning text completion, translation, and QA, where repeating memorised text and concept is not the desired behaviour. An example in MemoTrap is composed by a prompt (e.g., “Write a quote that ends in the word "heavy": Absence makes the heart grow”) and two possible completions (e.g., “heavy” and “fonder”), and the model needs to follow the instruction in the prompt in a zero-shot setting. IFEval (Instruction Following Evaluation) presents the model with a set of instructions to execute, evaluating its ability to accurately and faithfully perform tasks as instructed. An IFEval instance is composed by a prompt (e.g., Write a 300+ word summary of the wikipedia page [..]. Do not use any commas and highlight at least 3 sections that have titles in markdown format, for example [..]”), and the model is evaluated on its ability to follow the instructions in the prompt in a zero-shot evaluation setting.

Fact-Checking. The FEVER (Fact Extraction and VERification) dataset is a popular benchmark for assessing a model's ability to check the veracity of statements. Each instance in FEVER is composed of a claim (e.g., “Nikolaj Coster-Waldau worked with the Fox Broadcasting Company.”) and a label among SUPPORTS, REFUTES, and NOT ENOUGH INFO. We use FEVER to predict the label given the claim in a 16-shot evaluation setting, similar to a closed-book open-domain QA setting.

Hallucination Detection. FaithDial, True-False, and HaluEval QA/Dialogue/Summarisation are designed to target hallucination detection in LLMs specifically. FaithDial involves detecting faithfulness in dialogues: each instance in FaithDial consists of some background knowledge (e.g., “Dylan's Candy Bar is a chain of boutique candy shops [..]”), a dialogue history (e.g., "I love candy, what's a good brand?"), an original response from the Wizards of Wikipedia dataset (e.g., “Dylan's Candy Bar is a great brand of candy”), an edited response (e.g., “I don't know how good they are, but Dylan's Candy Bar has a chain of candy shops in various cities.”), and a set of BEGIN and VRM tags. We consider the task of predicting if the instance has the BEGIN tag “Hallucination” in an 8-shot setting. The True-False dataset aims to assess the model's ability to distinguish between true and false statements, covering several topics (cities, inventions, chemical elements, animals, companies, and scientific facts): in True-False, given a statement (e.g., “The giant anteater uses walking for locomotion.”) the model needs to identify whether it is true or not, in an 8-shot learning setting. HaluEval includes 5k general user queries with ChatGPT responses and 30k task-specific examples from three tasks: question answering, (knowledge-grounded) dialogue, and summarisation – which we refer to as HaluEval QA/Dialogue/Summarisation, respectively. In HaluEval QA, the model is given a question (e.g., “Which magazine was started first Arthur's Magazine or First for Women?”), a knowledge snippet (e.g., “Arthur's Magazine (1844–1846) was an American literary periodical published in Philadelphia in the 19th century.First for Women is a woman's magazine published by Bauer Media Group in the USA.”), and an answer (e.g., “First for Women was started first.”), and the model needs to predict whether the answer contains hallucinations in a zero-shot setting. HaluEval Dialogue and Summarisation follow a similar format.

Self-Consistency. SelfCheckGPT operates on the premise that when a model is familiar with a concept, its generated responses are likely to be similar and factually accurate. Conversely, for hallucinated information, responses tend to vary and contradict each other. In the SelfCheckGPT benchmark of the leaderboard, each LLM is tasked with generating six Wikipedia passages, each beginning with specific starting strings for individual evaluation instances. Among these six passages, the first one is generated with a temperature setting of 0.0, while the remaining five are generated with a temperature setting of 1.0. Subsequently, SelfCheckGPT-NLI, based on the trained “potsawee/deberta-v3-large-mnli” NLI model, assesses whether all sentences in the first passage are supported by the other five passages. If any sentence in the first passage has a high probability of being inconsistent with the other five passages, that instance is marked as a hallucinated sample. There are a total of 238 instances to be evaluated in this benchmark.

The benchmarks in the Hallucinations Leaderboard offer a comprehensive evaluation of an LLM's ability to handle several types of hallucinations, providing invaluable insights for AI/NLP researchers and developers/

Our comprehensive evaluation process gives a concise ranking of LLMs, allowing users to understand the performance of various models in a more comparative, quantitative, and nuanced manner. We believe that the Hallucinations Leaderboard is an important and ever more relevant step towards making LLMs more reliable and efficient, encouraging the development of models that can better understand and replicate human-like text generation while minimizing the occurrence of hallucinations.

The leaderboard is available at this link – you can submit models by clicking on Submit, and we will be adding analytics functionalities in the upcoming weeks. In addition to evaluation metrics, to enable qualitative analyses of the results, we also share a sample of generations produced by the model, available here.

We are currently in the process of evaluating a very large number of models from the Hugging Face Hub – we can analyse some of the preliminary results. For example, we can draw a clustered heatmap resulting from hierarchical clustering of the rows (datasets and metrics) and columns (models) of the results matrix.

We can identify the following clusters among models: Mistral 7B-based models (Mistral 7B-OpenOrca, zephyr 7B beta, Starling-LM 7B alpha, Mistral 7B Instruct, etc.) LLaMA 2-based models (LLaMA2 7B, LLaMA2 7B Chat, LLaMA2 13B, Wizard Vicuna 13B, etc.) Mostly smaller models (BLOOM 560M, GPT-Neo 125m, GPT-Neo 2.7B, Orca Mini 3B, etc.)

Let’s look at the results a bit more in detail.

Models based on Mistral 7B are by far more accurate than all other models on TriviaQA (8-shot) and TruthfulQA, while Falcon 7B seems to yield the best results so far on NQ (8-shot). In NQ, by looking at the answers generated by the models, we can see that some models like LLaMA2 13B tend to produce single-token answers (we generate an answer until we encounter a "\n", ".", or ","), which does not seem to happen, for example, with Falcon 7B. Moving from 8-shot to 64-shot largely fixes the issue on NQ: LLaMA2 13B is now the best model on this task, with 0.34 EM.

Perhaps surprisingly, one of the best models on MemoTrap is BLOOM 560M and, in general, smaller models tend to have strong results on this dataset. As the Inverse Scaling Prize evidenced, larger models tend to memorize famous quotes and therefore score poorly in this task. Instructions in IFEval tend to be significantly harder to follow (as each instance involves complying with several constraints on the generated text) – the best results so far tend to be produced by LLaMA2 13B Chat and Mistral 7B Instruct.

In summarisation, we consider two types of metrics: n-gram overlap with the gold summary (ROUGE1, ROUGE2, and ROUGE-L) and faithfulness of the generated summary wrt. the original document (factKB, BERTScore-Precision). When looking at rouge ROUGE-based metrics, one of the best models we have considered so far on CNN/DM is GPT JT 6B. By glancing at some model generations (available here), we can see that this model behaves almost extractively by summarising the first sentences of the whole document. Other models, like LLaMA2 13B, are not as competitive. A first glance at the model outputs, this happens because such models tend to only generate a single token – maybe due to the context exceeding the maximum context length.

On RACE, the most accurate results so far are produced on models based on Mistral 7B and LLaMA2. In SQuADv2, there are two settings: answerable (HasAns) and unanswerable (NoAns) questions. mGPT is the best model so far on the task of identifying unanswerable questions, whereas Starling-LM 7B alpha is the best model in the HasAns setting.

We consider two hallucination detection tasks, namely SelfCheckGPT — which checks if a model produces self-consistent answers — and HaluEval, which checks whether a model can identify faithfulness hallucinations in QA, Dialog, and Summarisation tasks with respect to a given snippet of knowledge. For SelfCheckGPT, the best-scoring model so far is Mistral 7B OpenOrca; one reason this happens is that this model always generates empty answers which are (trivially) self-consistent with themselves. Similarly, DiscoResearch/mixtral-7b-8expert produces very similar generations, yielding high self-consistency results. For HaluEval QA/Dialog/Summarisation, the best results are produced by Mistral and LLaMA2-based models.

The Hallucinations Leaderboard is an open effort to address the challenge of hallucinations in LLMs. Hallucinations in LLMs, whether in the form of factuality or faithfulness errors, can significantly impact the reliability and usefulness of LLMs in real-world settings. By evaluating a diverse range of LLMs across multiple benchmarks, the Hallucinations Leaderboard aims to provide insights into the generalisation properties and limitations of these models and their tendency to generate hallucinated content.

This initiative wants to aid researchers and engineers in identifying the most reliable models, and potentially drive the development of LLMs towards more accurate and faithful language generation. The Hallucinations Leaderboard is an evolving project, and we welcome contributions (fixes, new datasets and metrics, computational resources, ideas, ...) and feedback: if you would like to work with us on this project, remember to reach out!

#11087. Accelerate StarCoder with 🤗 Optimum Intel on Xeon: Q8/Q4 and Speculative Decoding

Recently, code generation models have become very popular, especially with the release of state-of-the-art open-source models such as BigCode’s StarCoder and Meta AI’s Code Llama. A growing number of works focuses on making Large Language Models (LLMs) more optimized and accessible. In this blog, we are happy to share the latest results of LLM optimization on Intel Xeon focusing on the popular code generation LLM, StarCoder.

The StarCoder Model is a cutting-edge LLM specifically designed for assisting the user with various coding tasks such as code completion, bug fixing, code summarization, and even generating code snippets from natural language descriptions. The StarCoder model is a member of the StarCoder family which includes the StarCoderBase variant as well. These Large Language Models for Code (Code LLMs) are trained on permissively licensed data from GitHub, including over 80 programming languages, Git commits, GitHub issues, and Jupyter notebooks. In this work we show more than 7x inference acceleration of StarCoder-15B model on Intel 4th generation Xeon by integrating 8bit and 4bit quantization with assisted generation.

Try out our demo on Hugging Face Spaces that is being run on a 4th Generation Intel Xeon Scalable processor.

We establish our baseline using StarCoder (15B) coupled with PyTorch and Intel Extension for PyTorch (IPEX). There are several datasets designed to evaluate the quality of automated code completion. In this work, we use the popular HumanEval dataset to evaluate the model’s quality and performance. HumanEval consists of 164 programming problems, in the form of a function signature with a docstring and the model completes the function’s code. The average length of the prompt is 139. We measure the quality using Bigcode Evaluation Harness and report the pass@1 metric. We measure model performance by measuring the Time To First Token (TTFT) and Time Per Output Token (TPOT) on the HumanEval test set and report the average TTFT and TPOT. The 4th generation Intel Xeon processors feature AI infused acceleration known as Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel® AMX). Specifically, it has built-in BFloat16 (BF16) and Int8 GEMM accelerators in every core to accelerate deep learning training and inference workloads. AMX accelerated inference is introduced through PyTorch 2.0 and Intel Extension for PyTorch (IPEX) in addition to other optimizations for various common operators used in LLM inference (e.g. layer normalization, SoftMax, scaled dot product). As the starting point we use out-of-the-box optimizations in PyTorch and IPEX to perform inference using a BF16 model. Figure 1 shows the latency of the baseline model and Tables 1 and 2 show its latency as well as its accuracy.

Text generation in LLMs is performed in an auto-regressive manner thus requiring the entire model to be loaded from memory to the CPU for each new token generation. We find that the bandwidth between the off-chip memory (DRAM) and the CPU poses the biggest bottleneck in the token generation process. Quantization is a popular approach for mitigating this issue. It reduces model size and hence decreases model weights loading time.

In this work we focus on two types of quantization:

SmoothQuant is a post training quantization algorithm that is used to quantize LLMs for INT8 with minimal accuracy loss. Static quantization methods were shown to be underperforming on LLMs due to large magnitude outliers found in specific channels of the activations. Since activations are quantized token-wise, static quantization results in either truncated outliers or underflowed low-magnitude activations. SmoothQuant algorithm solves this problem by introducing a pre-quantization phase where additional smoothing scaling factors are applied to both activations and weights which smooths the outliers in the activations and ensures better utilization of the quantization levels.

Figure 2. Computation diagram for INT8 static quantization.

Using IPEX, we apply SmoothQuant to the StarCoder model. We used the test split of the MBPP dataset as our calibration dataset and introduced Q8-StarCoder. Our evaluation shows that Q8-StarCoder holds no accuracy loss over the baseline (if fact, there is even a slight improvement). In terms of performance, Q8-StarCoder achieves ~2.19x speedup in TTFT and ~2.20x speedup in TPOT. Figure 3 shows the latency (TPOT) of Q8-StarCoder compared to the BF16 baseline model.

Figure 3. Latency speedup of 8-bit quantized model.

Although INT8 decreases the model size by 2x compared to BF16 (8 bits per weight compared to 16 bits), the memory bandwidth is still the largest bottleneck. To further decrease the model’s loading time from the memory, we quantized the model’s weights to 4 bits using WOQ. Note that 4bit WOQ requires dequantization to 16bit before the computation (Figure 4) which means that there is a compute overhead.

Figure 4. Computation diagram for model quantized to INT4.

Tensor-wise asymmetric Round To Nearest (RTN) quantization, a basic WOQ technique, poses challenges and often results in accuracy reduction, however it was shown in the literature (Zhewei Yao, 2022) that groupwise quantization of the model’s weights helps in retaining accuracy. To avoid accuracy degradation, we perform 4-bit quantization in groups (e.g. 128) of consequent values along the input channel, with scaling factors calculated per group. We found that groupwise 4bit RTN is sufficient to retain StarCoder’s accuracy on the HumanEval dataset. The 4bit model achieves 3.35x speedup in TPOT compared to the BF16 baseline (figure 5), however it suffers from expected slowdown of 0.84x in TTFT (Table 1) due to the overhead of dequantizing the 4bit to 16bit before computation.

Figure 5. Latency speedup of 4-bit quantized model.

The initial step of generating the first token, which involves parallel processing of the entire input prompt, demands significant computational resources when the prompt length is high. Computation, therefore, becomes the bottleneck in this stage. Hence, switching from BF16 to INT8 precision for this process improves the performance compared to the baseline (and to 4bit WOQ which involves compute overhead in the form of dequantization). However, starting from the second step, when the system generates the rest of the tokens one by one in an autoregressive manner, the model is loaded from the memory again and again for each new generated token. As a result, the bottleneck becomes memory bandwidth, rather than the number of calculations (FLOPS) performed and therefore INT4 outperforms INT8 and BF16.

Another method to mitigate the high inference latency and alleviate the memory bandwidth bottleneck issue is Assisted generation (AG) which is a practical implementation of speculative decoding. AG mitigates this issue by better balancing memory and computational operations. It relies on the premise that a smaller and faster assistant draft model often generates the same tokens as a larger target model.

AG uses a small, fast draft model to greedily generate K candidate tokens. These output tokens are generated much faster, but some of them may not resemble the output tokens of the original target model. Hence, in the next step, the target model checks the validity of all K candidate tokens in parallel in a single forward pass. This process speeds up the decoding since the latency of parallel decoding of K tokens is smaller than generating K tokens autoregressively.

For accelerating StarCoder, we use bigcode/tiny_starcoder_py as the draft model. This model shares a similar architecture with StarCoder but includes only 164M parameters - ~95x smaller than StarCoder, and thus much faster. To achieve an even greater speedup, in addition to quantizing the target model, we apply quantization to the draft model as well. We consider both 8bit SmoothQuant and 4bit WOQ quantization for the draft and target models. When evaluating both quantization options for the draft and target models, we found that 8bit SmoothQuant for both models yielded the best results: ~7.30x speedup in TPOT (Figure 6).

These quantization choices are backed up by the following observations:

Figure 6. Latency speedup of optimized model.

Table 1: Accuracy and latency measurements of the StarCoder model on Intel 4th Gen Xeon

To load the resulting models and run inference, you can just replace your AutoModelForXxx class with the corresponding IPEXModelForXxx class from optimum-intel.

#11045. HTML Semantics in Practice: Building More Accessible and Maintainable Web Pages

HTML remains the foundation of the modern web, but writing effective HTML involves more than placing elements on a page. The way developers structure content affects accessibility, maintainability, browser behavior, and how easily other developers can understand a project.

Semantic HTML provides a practical way to improve these areas without adding unnecessary JavaScript or relying on complex frameworks. By choosing elements according to their intended meaning, developers can create interfaces that are easier to navigate, maintain, and extend.

This article explores how semantic HTML works, why it matters, and how developers can apply it to real-world projects.

Semantic HTML uses elements that describe the purpose of their content. For example,

identifies a navigation section,
identifies the primary content, and
represents a self-contained piece of content.

These elements communicate meaning to browsers, assistive technologies, and developers who work with the code.

Consider a basic navigation menu built entirely with generic elements:

Although this code can work visually, it does not explicitly identify the navigation region.

The second example communicates the purpose of the region more clearly. Screen reader users can identify it as navigation, while developers can understand its role without examining multiple CSS classes.

Semantic elements do not automatically make every interface accessible, but they provide a stronger foundation.

A well-structured document helps developers organize content consistently. HTML provides several elements that support this approach.

identifies a group of navigation links.

contains the primary content of the document.

groups related content, usually with a heading.

represents independently meaningful content.

contains supplementary information.

provides footer information for a page or section.

These elements should be selected according to their purpose rather than their default appearance.

For example, a blog page might use the following structure:

This example establishes a clear document hierarchy. CSS can control the layout independently, allowing the same semantic structure to support different visual designs.

Accessibility is easier to implement when developers use elements that already provide the required behavior.

For instance, a clickable

may look like a button, but it does not automatically provide the keyboard interaction and button semantics that users expect.

A native button is usually the better choice:

For a form submission, use an appropriate submit button:

The label is explicitly associated with the input, and the browser can validate the email field before submission. Server-side validation is still necessary because client-side validation alone cannot guarantee that submitted data is valid or trustworthy.

Developers should also maintain a logical heading hierarchy, provide meaningful alternative text for informative images, and ensure that interactive elements can be used with a keyboard.

Accessibility is not a final styling step. It should influence decisions from the beginning of development.

HTML describes document structure, while CSS controls visual presentation. Keeping these responsibilities separate makes code easier to maintain.

For example, avoid using obsolete presentation attributes or selecting elements solely because they happen to produce a particular visual effect.

This approach allows the design to change without rewriting the content structure. It also makes it easier to apply consistent styling across multiple components.

However, classes should describe meaningful styling or component roles rather than becoming an unnecessarily complicated naming system.

Developers sometimes introduce JavaScript for behavior that HTML already supports. This can increase implementation complexity and create additional accessibility requirements.

The

and elements, for example, provide a native disclosure component:

The browser handles the basic expand-and-collapse interaction without a custom event listener.

This does not mean native elements can replace every interactive component. A complex navigation system, autocomplete field, or application dashboard may require additional JavaScript. The important principle is to begin with the simplest native solution that meets the actual requirements.

Less custom code can mean fewer opportunities for interaction bugs, although the final implementation should still be tested across supported browsers.

HTML that appears correct in one browser is not necessarily well structured or accessible. Developers should validate markup and test actual user interactions rather than relying only on visual inspection.

A practical review process includes the following steps:

Validate the HTML. Use the W3C Markup Validation Service to identify markup errors and unexpected structures.

Check keyboard navigation. Verify that links, buttons, forms, and interactive controls can be operated without a mouse.

Inspect heading structure. Confirm that headings describe the content hierarchy rather than serving only as styling tools.

Test form behavior. Check labels, required fields, validation messages, and server-side handling.

Review responsive layouts. Ensure that content remains usable at narrow viewport widths and when text is enlarged.

Test with assistive technology. Where possible, use screen readers to understand how the page structure is announced.

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot identify every usability or accessibility problem. Manual testing remains an important part of the process.

Even experienced developers can introduce unnecessary complexity when choosing elements.

One common mistake is using

as a generic container for every group of elements. A section should represent a meaningful thematic grouping, generally identified by a heading. A
remains appropriate when no more specific semantic element fits.

Another mistake is selecting elements based on their default browser styling. A heading should be used because it represents a heading, not because it appears larger than a paragraph.

Developers should also avoid adding ARIA attributes unnecessarily. Native HTML semantics should generally be preferred, with ARIA used when additional accessible names, states, or relationships are required.

Finally, semantic HTML should not be treated as a substitute for CSS, JavaScript testing, or broader accessibility practices. Good markup is one part of a reliable interface, not a complete solution by itself.

Semantic HTML is a practical investment in the long-term quality of a website. Meaningful elements improve document structure, provide useful information to assistive technologies, and help developers understand and maintain their code.

The most effective approach is straightforward: use native HTML elements according to their intended purpose, separate structure from presentation, minimize unnecessary JavaScript, and test the resulting interface with real user interactions in mind.

These practices do not require a framework or an elaborate architecture. They require thoughtful decisions about the structure of the web pages developers build every day.

#11039. CSS Container Queries: Build Reusable Components That Adapt to Their Layout

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Responsive web design has traditionally relied on media queries to adjust layouts according to viewport dimensions. This approach works well for page-level changes, but it becomes less convenient when the same component appears in different parts of a website.

Consider a product card used on a desktop product page, a narrow sidebar, and a mobile shopping interface. The available space can differ significantly in each location, even when the browser window remains the same size. A viewport-based media query cannot always respond appropriately to these differences.

CSS container queries offer a more flexible solution. They allow components to adapt to the dimensions of their containing element rather than relying exclusively on the browser viewport.

For developers building reusable interfaces, this capability can simplify responsive styling and reduce the need for duplicated component-specific CSS.

A media query evaluates conditions such as viewport width, user preferences, or device capabilities. A container query, by contrast, can evaluate the size of a designated container.

This distinction is particularly useful when developing reusable UI components. Instead of asking whether the screen is wide enough, a component can ask whether the space available to it is sufficient for a particular layout.

To use size container queries, developers first establish a query container with the container-type property.

The inline-size value enables querying the container's available inline dimension. In common horizontal writing modes, this corresponds to its width.

Once the container is established, its descendants can respond to its size:

When the relevant container reaches the specified minimum inline size, the content changes to a two-column layout.

The important detail is that the query responds to the container, not directly to the viewport. A card inside a narrow sidebar can therefore retain its compact presentation even on a large desktop screen.

A product card is a practical example because the same component often appears in multiple layouts.

The

element represents a self-contained item, while the heading and link provide meaningful structure and navigation.

Next, add a default layout that works in narrow spaces:

This version stacks the image and text vertically, making it suitable for compact spaces.

A container query can introduce a horizontal arrangement when the component has enough room:

The card now has two possible presentations without requiring separate HTML for desktop and mobile.

One implementation detail deserves attention: the query container's dimensions depend on its parent layout. Developers should test the component inside realistic page structures, especially when using grid or flex layouts, to ensure the container receives the intended available space.

Container queries and media queries solve related but different problems. Neither replaces the other entirely.

A media query is appropriate when the entire page needs to change according to the viewport. A container query is useful when an individual component needs to respond to its local layout.

Combining both techniques often produces the clearest implementation. For example, a media query can change the overall dashboard grid, while container queries adjust individual dashboard cards as their panels expand or contract.

When a page contains several nested containers, named queries can make the intended relationship clearer.

The container shorthand assigns a name and establishes the container's query type.

Named containers are especially useful in larger projects where components have nested layouts. They make query intent easier to communicate and help avoid accidentally targeting an unintended eligible ancestor.

Developers should still choose container names carefully and keep component styles understandable. Container queries add flexibility, but an excessive number of nested rules can make a design system harder to maintain.

Although container queries are relatively straightforward, a few implementation details can create unexpected results.

Forgetting to establish a container: A size query needs an appropriate query container. Without one, the expected container-based styling will not apply.

Using viewport breakpoints for every component: This can create unnecessary coupling between reusable components and the overall page layout. Use container queries when local available space is the relevant condition.

Assuming every CSS property can be queried: Size container queries are designed around supported container features and conditions. Check the relevant specifications before assuming that arbitrary styles or element properties can be used as query conditions.

Ignoring fallback behavior: A component should have a sensible default layout before enhanced container-query styles are applied. Test the experience in the browsers your project supports.

Overcomplicating responsive rules: More breakpoints do not automatically produce better interfaces. Start with the component's content and introduce a layout change only when the available space justifies it.

Container queries are supported in modern browsers, but production projects should verify their target browser requirements using Can I Use and test the actual interface.

A useful testing process includes resizing parent containers independently of the viewport, checking long headings and translated text, and inspecting how images and controls behave at intermediate widths.

Developers should also test components inside different contexts rather than relying on a single demonstration page. A card that works in a full-width content area might behave differently inside a sidebar or a dashboard grid.

For reusable component libraries, isolated examples and visual regression tests can help identify unintended changes when responsive styles are updated.

CSS container queries give developers a practical way to build components that respond to the space available in their immediate layout. They are particularly valuable for product cards, dashboard widgets, reusable content blocks, and component libraries that must work across different page structures.

The most effective strategy is to use media queries for viewport-level decisions and container queries for component-level adaptation. With meaningful HTML, sensible default styles, and careful testing, developers can create responsive interfaces that are easier to reuse and maintain.

Container queries do not eliminate every responsive design challenge, but they provide a more component-oriented way to solve many of them with native CSS.

#11032. Optimizing Core Web Vitals: Real Fixes for Slow INP

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When you click a button and nothing appears to happen, a brief pause later makes the page respond.

People don’t report this as a bug, but they tend to feel more frustrated than when they arrived. This tiny pause is precisely what the Interaction to Next Paint (INP) metric was designed to measure. Since it replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024, it has become one of the most challenging metrics for many development teams to address.

Unlike Large Contentful Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift, which can often be improved with image optimizations and reserved boxes, INP is deeply connected to your JavaScript, event handlers, and rendering pipeline.

This guide explains how to identify the interactions that cause delays and the actual fixes that produce real change.

INP observes every click, tap, and key press during a visit and reports the slowest one.

It measures the time between the user’s input and the browser rendering the next frame. On pages with many interactions, one extreme outlier is ignored.

Google’s performance thresholds are straightforward: 200 milliseconds or less is excellent, 200 to 500 milliseconds needs improvement, and anything over 500 milliseconds is poor.

These thresholds are based on the 75th percentile of real user visits, so performance on a fast laptop doesn’t tell the full story. Instead, the slow phone on a poor connection is what matters.

Each interaction is broken into three separate parts:

• Input delay: the time before the event handler can start, usually because the main thread is occupied with another task.

• Processing time: the time the event handler takes to run.

• Presentation delay: the time the browser spends recalculating styles, laying out the page, and painting.

Understanding which part of the interaction is causing the slowdown helps save time and effort, since each part can be addressed differently.

Lab-based tools like Lighthouse cannot interact with a site the way actual users do, so they may miss INP issues entirely.

It’s better to begin with real-user data. The Chrome UX Report and the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console can show you whether there are problems, and on which URLs.

To determine which interaction is slow, use Google’s open-source web-vitals library and its attribution build:

This pattern of using request Animation Frame followed by set Timeout ensures the browser completes the rendering before handling the analytics event.

It may seem odd, but it reliably delays the work until after the next frame. Also, be cautious of synchronous reads and writes to local Storage in event handlers, as they can block the main thread and accumulate more quickly than expected.

Sometimes your JavaScript is fast, yet the page still feels slow.

This is called presentation delay and is usually caused by too much DOM or too much layout work, or both.

Several changes can greatly improve performance:

Use virtualization for long lists so only the visible rows exist in the DOM.

Combine it with contain-intrinsic-size to prevent scrollbars from jumping.

Instead, batch all your layout reads first and then perform all your writes.

In a performance trace, wide purple blocks labeled "Recalculate Style" or "Layout" after your handler are a sign that you're facing this issue.

Fix 4: Keep Third-Party Scripts on a Leash

Tag managers, chat widgets, A/B testing tools, and ad scripts all compete for the same main thread as your code.

These scripts are a major cause of high input delay. Since you don't control their code, the main fix is usually about when they load, not how they work.

Load them using a sync or defer, delay non-essential scripts until after the first user interaction or during the page's idle time, and regularly audit them.

It's surprisingly common to find scripts that were added for a campaign years ago and are no longer needed. Removing such widgets can significantly improve performance.

#11026. TypeScript Discriminated Unions: Refactoring Boolean Flags into State Machines

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prerequisites: Code samples require TypeScript 4.0 or later and a tsconfig.json with "target": "ES2016" or higher and "strict": true. The FormState recursive type alias requires TypeScript 3.7+.

Boolean flags paired with optional fields are a common source of impossible-state bugs in TypeScript codebases. Discriminated unions eliminate these invalid states at compile time, so the compiler rejects objects that combine fields illegally. This article traces the pattern from its simplest form through a common the pitfalls of building members from booleans and into a fully typed multi-step form state machine with an exhaustive reducer.

Consider a common pattern: a response object shaped as { success: boolean; data?: string[] }, where data exists only when success is true. TypeScript cannot enforce this relationship. The type system sees data as string[] | undefined regardless of the value of success, because both fields belong to a single interface. Nothing prevents a caller from constructing { success: true } with no data, or { success: false, data: ['oops'] }.

The non-null assertion hides the real problem. The type permits a state that the business logic considers impossible, and the compiler cannot help.

Control-flow narrowing in TypeScript operates on the type of the property being checked, not the shape of the enclosing object. When the type is a single interface rather than a union, checking if (res.success) narrows res.success from boolean to true within that branch, but it does not change the type of res itself. The object's shape remains ApiResponse, and data stays string[] | undefined. To narrow an object's shape, its type must be a union of distinct types in the first place. Without that union, the compiler has nothing to narrow to.

Discriminated unions combine multiple object types that share a common property whose type is a unique string, number, or boolean literal in each variant. This shared property is called the discriminant property. The pattern is also known as a tagged union or algebraic data type. When code branches on the discriminant, TypeScript narrows the entire object to the specific variant, making all fields of that variant available without assertions.

The compiler rejects the impossible state entirely. If success is true, data must be present. If success is false, providing data causes a type error.

A different construction problem shows up when a union member is built from a runtime boolean. A variable typed boolean is the union true | false, and the object { b: flag, c: value } has to fit one member of Result below. Before TypeScript 3.5 the compiler rejected that assignment (I confirmed the error on 3.4.5). Since 3.5 it accepts it when the discriminant is a boolean or another small union of literals, so on a current compiler the code in the comment below compiles.

That acceptance is a convenience, not a guarantee that the object is valid. The accepted object can still carry c when b is false. Building each variant in its own branch keeps the data honest and works on every version. If you support older compilers, you will also see the old error in existing Stack Overflow answers.

The first option builds each variant in its own branch. Each branch returns an object literal that matches exactly one union member, so c only exists when b is true. The second option uses a generic type parameter constrained to true | false, allowing the compiler to resolve the correct branch based on the argument's literal type at each call site. A runtime guard protects against callers passing a widened boolean value, which can bypass the compile-time conditional rest type guarantee (a boolean-typed argument makes the rest type [c: number] | []).

switch on a discriminant property narrows the union to exactly one variant per case block. Each case branch sees only the fields defined for that variant. While if/else if chains work identically for narrowing purposes, switch is the conventional choice for tagged unions because it maps one branch per variant and integrates naturally with exhaustiveness checking via a default clause.

When a unique property exists only in one variant, the in operator can narrow without a dedicated discriminant field. Checking if ('data' in obj) narrows to the variant containing data. However, this approach is less explicit, harder to exhaust systematically, and breaks when two variants share a property name, since the in check can no longer distinguish between them. Use it to supplement, not replace, literal discriminants.

This example demonstrates discriminated union narrowing outside of object configuration patterns. It uses Number() rather than parseInt to correctly reject strings with trailing non-numeric characters ('42abc' → NaN) and to preserve decimal values ('3.14' → 3.14). The discriminated return type forces callers to handle both outcomes explicitly.

Exhaustiveness means branching logic handles every member of a union. When a new variant is added to the union, the compiler flags all unhandled cases. Without exhaustiveness, adding a variant silently falls through existing branches, typically into a default case that was written for a different set of states, producing runtime errors that surface only after refactors reach production.

The canonical exhaustiveness technique places an assertNever function in the default branch of a switch. If every variant is handled, the remaining type in default is never. If a variant is missed, the type is not never, and the assignment to the never parameter fails at compile time. In a pure TypeScript codebase this line is unreachable at runtime; it guards against JavaScript callers or unsafe type assertions that bypass compile-time checking.

The error appears the moment the code compiles, before any test runs. Adding case 'triangle' resolves it and restores exhaustiveness.

A FormState type with a kind discriminant models each step as a distinct variant. Each variant carries only the data relevant to that step, making impossible combinations unrepresentable. The FormState type uses a recursive type alias (supported since TypeScript 3.7) to allow the error variant to reference FormState itself.

The step2 variant includes validated step1Data, ensuring that reaching step two without completing step one is structurally impossible. The error variant carries lastState for retry logic, but excludes nested errors via Exclude.

Actions model the transitions between states. Each action is its own tagged union member. The NEXT action is split into step-specific variants so that each transition carries only the data relevant to its source step, preventing structurally incomplete payloads.

The reducer uses nested switch statements. The outer switch dispatches on state.kind, the inner on action.type where multiple actions apply to a single state. Both levels use assertNever to guarantee exhaustiveness.

Each inner switch must enumerate every member of FormAction, either as a handled transition or an explicit no-op, for the default branch to see never. This verbosity is the cost of the pattern, and it pays for itself: adding a new action type to FormAction produces compile errors in every inner switch that does not list it.

A flat alternative like { step: number; isSubmitting: boolean; error?: string; data?: object } permits states that should never exist: isSubmitting: true with error defined simultaneously, step: 3 with no data from steps one or two, or error populated while isSubmitting remains true. With the flat type, you write guards like if (state.isSubmitting && !state.error) at every consumption site. The discriminated union eliminates these guards structurally. Adding a sixth state to the union triggers compile errors everywhere the reducer and any consuming code fails to handle it.

The ?: never pattern works by marking a property as optional with type never, which prevents any non-undefined value from being assigned; undefined remains assignable unless exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true is set in tsconfig.json. It is useful for lightweight exclusive-field constraints but provides none of the narrowing or exhaustiveness guarantees that discriminated unions offer.

Discriminated unions fit well in these scenarios:

Two-variant unions also get compile-time exhaustiveness and narrowing from the pattern, as the ApiResponse example earlier demonstrates.

Using string instead of a string literal for the discriminant defeats narrowing entirely. With kind: string on every variant, switch (x.kind) does not narrow the union, so reading a variant-only field such as x.a inside case 'a' fails with error TS2339 (property does not exist on the union).

Building union members from a runtime boolean without branching can produce objects that carry fields the other variant should not have, even when the compiler accepts it (see above).

Nesting unions more than one level deep (a discriminated union inside another discriminated union) complicates narrowing and makes reducers harder to read. Prefer flat discriminants with descriptive kind values like 'step2-loading' over nested structures.

Boolean flags hide impossible states behind runtime assumptions. Discriminated unions surface those states at compile time, and exhaustive checking with assertNever ensures that future additions to the union cannot silently slip through existing code paths.

Find one boolean-flag type in your codebase, refactor it into a discriminated union, and let the compiler reveal every location that assumed an impossible state was safe.

#11020. Next.js Caching: How to Fix revalidate Failures and Stale Data

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This article targets Next.js 15.1+, App Router only. Caching behavior differs in Next.js 13 and 14; consult the relevant migration guides if you are on an earlier version.

Stale data that ignores revalidate is one of the most common Next.js support issues. A developer sets revalidate = 60, deploys to production, and pages never reflect the latest content. Or worse, a page that was serving perfectly valid content silently transforms into a cached 404. When Next.js caching revalidate is not working, the root cause is rarely a single misconfiguration. It is nearly always an interaction between multiple cache layers, each with its own lifetime and invalidation logic.

The Next.js App Router maintains four distinct caching mechanisms: the Router Cache (client-side, in-memory), the Full Route Cache (server-side rendered HTML and RSC payload), the Data Cache (individual fetch response storage), and Request Memoization (per-request deduplication). A page can appear stale because any one of these layers holds an outdated response, and diagnosing the responsible layer requires systematic work.

This article walks through the most common reasons ISR revalidation fails, exposes a documented but underappreciated pattern where transient upstream outages produce permanently cached 404s, and provides a copy-paste-safe data-fetching helper that prevents it. A diagnostic decision tree is included as a reference for debugging future issues.

Understanding why next.js ISR stale data appears requires knowing where cached content lives.

Next.js stores individual fetch responses in the Data Cache, keyed by URL and request options. When a fetch call includes next: { revalidate: 60 }, the Data Cache holds that response for 60 seconds before marking it stale. Next.js persists this cache across requests and deployments on platforms like Vercel.

The Full Route Cache stores the complete rendered output of a route, both the HTML and the React Server Component payload. For statically generated routes, Next.js populates this cache at build time. For ISR routes, Next.js populates it on the first request and refreshes it according to the revalidate interval. This is the cache most developers think of when they configure ISR.

On the client side, the Router Cache lives entirely in-memory in the browser. In Next.js 15 the staleTimes defaults are 0 seconds for dynamic pages (not cached) and 5 minutes for static pages and fully prefetched links; 14.x used 30 seconds for dynamic pages (source: Next.js docs, staleTimes). Check the values for your installed version. A page might be fresh on the server but stale in the Router Cache, leading to confusion during manual testing.

A page can be "correct" in the Data Cache but outdated in the Full Route Cache, or fresh on the server but stale in the client's Router Cache. Each layer must be considered independently during debugging.

Next.js ISR follows a stale-while-revalidate model. When a request arrives for a page whose revalidate interval has elapsed, Next.js serves the existing cached page immediately to the visitor. Simultaneously, it triggers a background re-render of the page.

If the background render succeeds, the newly rendered page replaces the old cached page. Subsequent visitors receive the fresh content.

If it throws an error, Next.js retains the previously cached page and logs the error. The stale page keeps serving, which is generally the desired behavior during transient failures.

If the background render calls notFound(), however, the behavior changes in a way that catches many developers off guard. This is where the 404 caching trap lives, and it is the single most damaging failure mode in ISR.

The most frequent cause of nextjs revalidate not working is a configuration conflict between route-segment-level settings and fetch-level settings. Within a segment tree, the lowest export const revalidate value wins. However, fetch-level next: { revalidate } settings apply per-request and can differ from the segment default. A missing value on a nested segment can silently inherit from the parent, producing unexpected intervals.

More subtly, mixing fetch-level caching directives with route-segment config can cause one to override the other entirely:

Setting cache: 'no-store' on a fetch call opts that fetch out of the Data Cache and causes the route to be treated as dynamic, bypassing the Full Route Cache. The segment-level export const revalidate cannot override a no-store directive on an individual fetch.

The quickest diagnostic is checking the build output. Next.js marks each route in build output with symbols indicating static or dynamic status. In Next.js 13/14, ○ indicates static and λ indicates dynamic. Next.js 15 prints ○ for static, ● for SSG with params and ƒ for dynamic routes; the legend printed at the end of next build lists the symbols for your installed version. If a route expected to be statically generated shows a dynamic indicator, something in its render path is triggering dynamic behavior.

Even when Next.js caching is configured correctly, your deployment platform may override these headers. Vercel, Cloudflare, and self-hosted setups each add their own Cache-Control headers. A CDN s-maxage value that outlives the revalidate interval will serve stale HTML from the CDN edge regardless of whether Next.js has regenerated the page on the origin.

The x-nextjs-cache response header is an essential debugging signal. It returns HIT when the response comes from cache, STALE when the cached response is being served while revalidation occurs in the background, and MISS when the page is rendered fresh. If this header shows STALE but the page content never updates, the problem is likely upstream in a CDN layer. The x-nextjs-cache header is reliably emitted on Vercel. On self-hosted deployments, confirm your reverse proxy forwards it.

revalidatePath purges the Full Route Cache for a specific path, while revalidateTag invalidates all cached fetch responses and unstable_cache entries tagged with a specific string. Using the wrong granularity, or forgetting to tag fetch calls, is a common source of next.js cache not updating.

Another subtle issue: protect on-demand revalidation routes with a shared secret token to prevent unauthorized cache purges. Both revalidatePath and revalidateTag return void, so there is no result to check. Wrap the calls in try/catch and log caught errors. In Next.js 16, revalidateTag takes a second profile argument (the docs recommend "max") and the one-argument form is deprecated.

The notFound() function internally throws a special error to signal a 404 response. This is an internal implementation detail subject to change; rely on the documented behavior described in the Next.js notFound API reference, not on the internal error string. Its behavior depends on when it is called during the rendering lifecycle.

During prerendering or static generation, calling notFound() causes Next.js to serve a static 404 page with a 404 HTTP status code and cache that 404 as the route's canonical response.

Inside a Suspense boundary after streaming has already begun, Next.js cannot change the HTTP status code because headers have already been sent with a 200 status. Instead, it injects a tag into the response. This is a subtly different failure mode: the page appears to load successfully to the browser but tells search engines to deindex it, potentially causing SEO damage that goes undetected for multiple crawl cycles, depending on your site's crawl frequency. This behavior is documented in the Next.js notFound API reference.

A closely related failure mode is how a transient ISR error can cache a 404, turning a momentary backend hiccup into a permanently cached not-found response.

This is the next.js notFound caching trap, and it follows a predictable sequence:

I reproduced this on Next.js 15.5.28 with next build && next start, a page with revalidate = 3, and a local CMS stub I switched to returning 500. When the page called notFound() on the failed fetch, the next response was a 404 served from the cache (x-nextjs-cache: HIT), and it stayed a 404 until a later revalidation succeeded after the stub came back. When the same page threw an error instead, every response kept serving the previous good page through the outage. Your platform and version may differ, so test it on yours.

Never let a transient upstream failure produce a notFound() call. Throw an error instead, and let Next.js serve the stale page while logging the failure so you can investigate.

When debugging stale pages or unexpected 404s, work through the following decision path:

Step 2: Inspect cache headers. Does the x-nextjs-cache header show HIT, STALE, or MISS? If STALE persists, check whether background revalidation is failing silently. If the header is absent, a CDN or reverse proxy may be stripping it.

Step 3: Verify revalidate config. Is revalidate set at the correct level (page, layout, or fetch)? Are there conflicting values? Does any fetch call use cache: 'no-store'?

Step 4: Check data-fetch error handling. Does the code call notFound() when upstream data is null? If so, a transient CMS outage can produce a cached 404. This is the most commonly reported branch for pages that "disappear" after working correctly.

Step 5: Verify on-demand revalidation. If using revalidatePath or revalidateTag, confirm the call completes without throwing by wrapping it in try/catch, and confirm that fetch calls are properly tagged.

Step 6: Check for middleware rewrites. Middleware (called Proxy in Next.js 16) that rewrites URLs can alter the cache key, causing revalidation to target a different cache entry than expected.

The core distinction is between "this resource genuinely does not exist" and "the upstream server is temporarily unreachable." The first case warrants notFound(). The second case should throw an error so that Next.js retains the previously cached good page and logs the failure.

A helper can encode this logic once and apply across every route in a project.

The helper returns null only when the upstream server explicitly responds with a 404 status (indicating the resource genuinely does not exist) or with 204/205 (no content). For 5xx errors, other non-OK responses (such as 401, 403, or 429), network failures, or malformed JSON bodies, it throws a structured FetchError, ensuring Next.js treats the revalidation as failed and continues serving the stale-but-valid cached page. All error messages log only the hostname, never the full URL, to prevent leaking secrets such as API keys in query parameters. A 10-second AbortController timeout prevents indefinitely hung requests from blocking ISR workers.

Note: The import below uses the @/ path alias. Ensure your tsconfig.json includes "paths": { "@/*": ["./*"] }, which is the default for create-next-app projects.

If fetchOrThrow throws due to a 500, another non-OK status, or a network error, the error bubbles up, the background revalidation fails, and Next.js serves the previously cached page. The failure is logged server-side for monitoring. Only a confirmed 404 from the upstream API triggers notFound().

Wrapping the helper with the "use cache" directive or unstable_cache provides an additional layer of control. "use cache" is experimental in Next.js 15 (behind experimental.dynamicIO) and stable in Next.js 16 with cacheComponents: true. unstable_cache is the option for Next.js 15 projects that want to stay off experimental flags. Tagging fetch calls enables precise on-demand invalidation through webhook-triggered API routes. A CMS webhook handler, for example, can call revalidateTag('posts') to purge all cached responses tagged with posts, forcing immediate regeneration on the next request without waiting for the revalidate interval.

When nextjs revalidate is not working, run through these checks in order:

Most "revalidate not working" issues trace back to one of three root causes: configuration conflicts between cache layers, accidental opt-in to dynamic rendering, or the notFound() caching trap that converts transient upstream failures into permanent 404s.

The single most important takeaway is this: never let a transient upstream failure produce a notFound() call. Throw an error instead, and let Next.js serve the stale page while logging the failure so you can investigate.

The fetchOrThrow helper encodes this logic in a pattern that can be adapted to any data source.

The diagnostic decision tree and debugging checklist above provide a systematic path through the most common failure modes. Bookmark them for the next time a production page goes stale or vanishes.
